title: How do you read a plan for common issues — a Seq Scan where an Index Scan was expected (missing index, non-sargable predicate, low selectivity), a Nested Loop with a huge outer table (consider Hash Join), Sort with high cost (missing index for ORDER BY), and vastly different estimated vs actual rows (stale statistics → `ANALYZE` the table)?
shortTitle: Reading a Query Plan for Common Performance Issues

s1_definition.profdef: Reading a query plan for common issues means pattern-matching the plan tree against a small set of known problem signatures: a Seq Scan appearing where an Index Scan was expected (missing index, non-sargable predicate, or low selectivity), a Nested Loop join driven by a huge outer table (where a Hash Join would be cheaper), a Sort node with high cost (an index could have supplied the ordering), and a large divergence between estimated and actual rows (stale statistics, fixed by running ANALYZE). Each signature maps to a specific remedy.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the plan as a bank clerk's written route for finding and sorting transactions. You scan that route for four telltale mistakes: the clerk flipping through the entire ledger when an index tab exists (Seq Scan where Index expected), the clerk re-checking the whole archive once per customer in a long list (Nested Loop with a huge outer), the clerk manually re-sorting a big pile by date when the ledger is already date-ordered (costly Sort), and the clerk badly under-guessing how many rows they will touch (stale statistics). Spotting each tells you exactly what to fix.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match the plan against four signatures — unexpected Seq Scan, Nested Loop on a huge outer, costly Sort, and estimate-versus-actual gap — each with a specific fix.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reading a query plan for common issues means pattern-matching the plan tree against a small set of known problem signatures: a Seq Scan appearing where an Index Scan was expected (missing index, non-sargable predicate, or low selectivity), a Nested Loop join driven by a huge outer table (where a Hash Join would be cheaper), a Sort node with high cost (an index could have supplied the ordering), and a large divergence between estimated and actual rows (stale statistics, fixed by running ANALYZE). Each signature maps to a specific remedy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the plan as a bank clerk's written route for finding and sorting transactions. You scan that route for four telltale mistakes: the clerk flipping through the entire ledger when an index tab exists (Seq Scan where Index expected), the clerk re-checking the whole archive once per customer in a long list (Nested Loop with a huge outer), the clerk manually re-sorting a big pile by date when the ledger is already date-ordered (costly Sort), and the clerk badly under-guessing how many rows they will touch (stale statistics). Spotting each tells you exactly what to fix.

**One line to remember:** Match the plan against four signatures — unexpected Seq Scan, Nested Loop on a huge outer, costly Sort, and estimate-versus-actual gap — each with a specific fix.

sections.s2_technical:
The first signature is a Seq Scan where you expected an Index Scan. This has three usual causes. There may simply be no index on the filtered column, so you add one. The predicate may be non-sargable, meaning it wraps the column in a function or does a leading-wildcard LIKE, like WHERE UPPER(account_id) = 'X' or WHERE name LIKE '%kumar', so the index cannot be used; you rewrite it to touch the bare column or add a functional index. Or the filter may be low-selectivity, matching most of the table, in which case the optimizer correctly prefers a scan and there is nothing to fix.

The second signature is a Nested Loop join with a huge outer table. A Nested Loop probes the inner table once per outer row, which is great when the outer side is tiny and the inner side is indexed, but catastrophic when the outer side has millions of rows. If you see that, a Hash Join — which builds a hash table of one side and streams the other through it once — is usually far cheaper. A bad Nested Loop often appears because the optimizer underestimated the outer row count, which circles back to statistics.

The third signature is a Sort node with high cost. If a query has ORDER BY and the plan shows an expensive Sort, an index on the ORDER BY columns could let the engine read rows already in order, turning the Sort into a cheap index traversal. The same applies to ordered operations behind GROUP BY and some merge joins.

The fourth signature, and the one that explains many of the others, is a large gap between estimated and actual rows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE. The optimizer makes every decision from table statistics; if those statistics are stale — say after a bulk load — it may estimate ten rows where there are ten million, pick a Nested Loop or an Index Scan that is wrong at the true size, and perform terribly. Running ANALYZE on the table refreshes the statistics, and the optimizer often picks a dramatically better plan afterward. Autovacuum normally keeps statistics fresh, but after large data changes a manual ANALYZE is wise.

The senior nuance is to read the plan bottom-up and inside-out, because the innermost nodes execute first, and to use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to tell whether the cost is CPU time or disk I/O.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: a report that joins accounts to transactions and sorts by date is slow, and the on-call engineer must diagnose it from the plan.

Problem 1 — a Seq Scan where an index was expected. We model a query whose predicate is non-sargable and show the plan reporting a Seq Scan, with the diagnosis attached.

Problem 2 — a Nested Loop with a huge outer. We model a join plan whose outer table is large and flag that a Hash Join would be cheaper.

Problem 3 — a costly Sort and a stale-statistics gap. We model a Sort node on ORDER BY created_at and a node whose estimate is far below actual, each with its remedy.

The code includes a PlanNode, a PlanDiagnostician that inspects a list of nodes and emits the specific remedy for each signature, and a demo that feeds a realistic problem plan through the diagnostician.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
plan-diagnostics-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/main/java/com/bank/plandiag/
│   ├── PlanDiagDemo.java
│   ├── plan/PlanNode.java
│   └── service/PlanDiagnostician.java
└── src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_tables.sql
```

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway)
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id          VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    txn_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
-- Fixes for the four signatures:
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_account ON transactions(account_id);        -- cure Seq Scan
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_created ON transactions(created_at);         -- cure costly Sort
-- ANALYZE transactions;   -- cure stale-stats estimate gap
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
diagnostics:
  big-outer-threshold: 1000000     # Nested Loop outer rows above this = switch to Hash Join
  stale-ratio: 100                 # actual > est*100 = stale statistics
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests
# Run
java -cp target/plan-diagnostics-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.plandiag.PlanDiagDemo

# Real PostgreSQL:
# EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT a.holder_name, t.amount
#   FROM accounts a JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id=a.id
#   WHERE UPPER(t.account_id)='SAV2001' ORDER BY t.created_at;
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a four-node plan for a slow join-and-sort report.

Step 1 — The first node is a Seq Scan on a column where an index was expected, and its predicate is non-sargable. The diagnostician reports the cause as a function-wrapped predicate and recommends rewriting it or adding a functional index.

Step 2 — The second node is a Nested Loop whose outer table has five million rows, far above the one-million threshold. The diagnostician recommends switching to a Hash Join.

Step 3 — The third node is a Sort. Because sorting five million rows is expensive and the query orders by created_at, the diagnostician recommends an index on created_at so the rows arrive already ordered.

Step 4 — The fourth node is an Index Scan whose estimate was 10 rows but whose actual was 5,000,000 — a hundred-thousand-fold gap, well over the stale ratio. The diagnostician recommends running ANALYZE to refresh statistics, which will likely fix the earlier Nested Loop choice too.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 17:36:00 [INFO] Diagnosing slow report plan...
2026-10-25 17:36:00 [WARNING] DIAGNOSIS: Seq Scan where Index expected → non-sargable predicate (function on column) → add index / rewrite predicate
2026-10-25 17:36:00 [WARNING] DIAGNOSIS: Nested Loop outer=5000000 (huge) → switch to Hash Join
2026-10-25 17:36:00 [WARNING] DIAGNOSIS: Costly Sort → add index on ORDER BY columns to avoid the sort
2026-10-25 17:36:00 [WARNING] DIAGNOSIS: Estimate 10 vs actual 5000000 → stale statistics → ANALYZE the table
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  EXPLAIN ANALYZE output (plan tree)
    │
    ▼
  PlanDiagnostician scans each node
    ├─ Seq Scan + indexExpected  → non-sargable? / missing index? / low selectivity?
    ├─ Nested Loop + outer>1M     → recommend Hash Join
    ├─ Sort node                  → recommend index on ORDER BY columns
    └─ actual > est×100           → recommend ANALYZE (stale stats)
          │
          ▼
  Findings list → each mapped to a concrete fix
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I read a query plan for performance problems I pattern-match it against four well-known signatures, and each one maps to a specific fix. The first is a sequential scan appearing where I expected an index scan. The three usual causes are a missing index on the filtered column, a non-sargable predicate that wraps the column in a function or uses a leading-wildcard LIKE so the index cannot be used, or a low-selectivity filter that matches so much of the table that the optimizer correctly prefers a scan. I add the index, rewrite the predicate to touch the bare column, or accept the scan accordingly.

The second signature is a Nested Loop join driven by a huge outer table. A Nested Loop probes the inner table once per outer row, which is fine when the outer side is tiny but disastrous when it has millions of rows, so I would expect a Hash Join there instead. The third is a Sort node with high cost: if the query orders by a column, an index on that column lets the engine read rows already in order and skip the sort entirely. The fourth, and the one that often explains the others, is a large gap between estimated and actual rows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE, because the optimizer makes every choice from table statistics, and if those are stale — typically after a bulk load — it can estimate ten rows where there are ten million and then choose a Nested Loop or an index path that is wrong at the true size. Running ANALYZE on the table refreshes the statistics and usually produces a far better plan.

In our National Bank of India reporting layer a join-and-sort report crawled; the plan showed all four symptoms at once — a Seq Scan from a UPPER-wrapped predicate, a Nested Loop over five million rows, a costly Sort on the transaction date, and an estimate of ten against an actual of five million. We rewrote the predicate to be sargable, added an index on the date column, and ran ANALYZE, after which the optimizer switched the join to a Hash Join and the sort disappeared, taking the report from minutes to seconds. I read plans bottom-up because the innermost nodes run first, and I use the BUFFERS option to see whether the pain is CPU or disk. The line I remember is to match the plan against four signatures — unexpected Seq Scan, Nested Loop on a huge outer, costly Sort, and a big estimate-versus-actual gap — each with its own concrete remedy.

---

keyPoints: EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE: see query execution plan
Look for: full table scans, missing indexes, sort operations
Optimize: add indexes, rewrite queries, reduce data scanned
Slow query log: identify queries exceeding threshold
